newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Institute cuts 1997 German growth outlook.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Institute cuts 1997 German growth outlook.

text.p: DIW, one of Germany's six leading economic institutes, on Tuesday lowered its forecast for 1997 growth to two percent and said Germany was likely to miss the deficit target for European monetary union (EMU).
DIW and its five peers had forecast as recently as October that 1997 growth in gross domestic product (GDP) would be 2.5 percent.
"The economic rebound of the past few years has been by far the weakest in the history of the Federal Republic of Germany," the DIW report said.

The Berlin-based think tank, closely affiliated with trade unions and the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), also said in its report it expects 1996 growth to be 1.5 percent, up from a November forecast of 1.25 percent.
The government is scheduled to release 1996 GDP data on Thursday.

DIW said Germany's public sector budget deficit is likely to be about 3.4 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year, down from 3.9 percent of GDP last year but above the 3.0 percent target for inclusion in the planned single European currency.
Data for 1997 are crucial as they will be the basis for deciding which countries will participate in European monetary union (EMU) at the planned start in January 1999.

The institute also said German unemployment could climb to a record 4.5 million. Unemployment in November 1996 was 3.942 million before seasonal adjustment. Jobless data for December are also due for release on Thursday.
"The longer it takes to achieve a sweeping change in the labour market, the less likely is it that the government will meet its goal of halving unemployment by the year 2000," the report said.
Companies' reluctance to invest means growth remains too low to create jobs and meet the challenges posed by German unification, it said.
Ernst Schwanhold, economic policy spokesman for the SPD parliamentary faction, said the new DIW forecast proved it was time for a turnaround in economic policy.
Bonn should go on the offensive, together with its European neighbours, to stimulate jobs and growth, he said.

"The DIW is right to demand of German economic policy that instead of chasing after a reduction in the state share of the economy, that it improve its management of the economy and the social system," Schwanhold said.
"The currency union must be linked to a jobs (creation) union," he said.
DIW said the growth slowdown in formerly communist east Germany was the biggest cause for concern.
Growth rates of four to five percent would be needed for the next several years for the east to reach a comparable level of prosperity with the west, it said.

But developments in the west have also been disappointing, DIW said. Since the end of the recession in 1993, the German economy has grown only 5.5 percent, far weaker than in the recovery of the early 1980s.
Domestic demand has not received the hoped-for boost from the export-driven recovery, it said.
